blocks.text: A client and server meeting for the first time have no guarantee they support the same features, one might understand resource subscriptions, the other might not have implemented that yet, one might support sampling, the other might not. Capability negotiation is the architectural process that resolves this upfront, during the very first exchange of a session, so that neither side ever has to guess what the other can actually do.
1. What Capability Negotiation Actually Is

blocks.alt: Client capabilities and server capabilities negotiate

blocks.text: Capability negotiation is the exchange, during initialization, of what each side declares it supports, followed by both sides using only the features that turned out to be supported by both. It is not a back-and-forth bargaining process, it happens in exactly one round trip, each side states its capabilities once, and that statement holds for the entire session.

blocks.title: Not a request for permission
blocks.content: Neither side asks the other for permission to have a capability, each side simply reports what it already has. There is nothing to grant or deny, only something to observe and then respect.

blocks.text: This one-shot design is deliberately simple compared to negotiation protocols found elsewhere that involve several rounds of proposal and counter-proposal, MCP's designers chose a flat, declarative exchange instead, trading some flexibility for a handshake that is easy to implement correctly and easy to reason about.

blocks.title: A quick framing
blocks.content: Negotiation here does not mean back and forth bargaining, it means each side simply states what it supports, once, and both sides then act accordingly.

blocks.text: 2. Where Negotiation Happens: The Initialize Exchange

blocks.alt: A client and server negotiate through the initialize exchange

blocks.text: Negotiation is carried entirely by the initialize request and its response, the same handshake that begins every session, as covered in Session Management. The client's capabilities travel in the request, the server's capabilities travel in the response, and once that response is received, negotiation is complete.

Because this all happens inside one request and one response, negotiation adds essentially no extra round trips to session startup, it rides entirely on a handshake that already had to happen anyway to establish the session in the first place.

It also means capability negotiation cannot be delayed or deferred, by the time initialized is sent and the session is considered active, both sides already have everything they need to know about what the other supports for the rest of that session's life.
3. What a Client Declares

A client's capabilities describe what it is able to do on the server's behalf, most notably whether it supports sampling, letting the server ask it to run a completion, and whether it supports receiving certain kinds of notifications. An empty capabilities object is a completely valid declaration, it simply means this client does not support any optional features beyond the baseline.

A client omitting a capability entirely is treated identically to declaring it as unsupported, there is no meaningful difference between an absent field and an explicit false, both simply mean the server should not expect that feature from this client.

A client with no special capabilities at all, one that never receives sampling requests and never needs any of the optional notification types, is a perfectly ordinary and common case, plenty of simple host implementations declare an essentially empty capabilities object and function correctly.
4. What a Server Declares

A server's capabilities describe which categories of functionality it exposes at all, tools, resources, prompts, and for resources specifically, whether it supports subscriptions and change notifications on top of simple reads.

The absence of a whole top-level category, no tools field at all in capabilities, tells the client that server has no tools to offer whatsoever, and the client should not bother calling tools/list against it.

A minimal server exposing only a handful of tools and nothing else declares just capabilities.tools and omits resources and prompts entirely, this is not treated as a lesser or incomplete server, it is simply a server with a narrower, and perfectly valid, feature set.
A server with a minimal feature set might declare only tools, while a full-featured one declares tools, resources, and prompts together, each visible plainly in this same negotiated object.
5. How Declared Capabilities Are Compared

blocks.alt: A client capability is compared against a server capability

blocks.text: There is no explicit matching algorithm running somewhere, comparison happens implicitly, each side simply checks the other's declared capabilities before attempting to use a feature that depends on them. A client checks the server's capabilities before calling resources/subscribe, a server checks the client's capabilities before sending a sampling request.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Feature being used","Capability checked before using it"],"rows":[["Resource subscriptions","Server's capabilities.resources.subscribe"],["Sampling request from server to client","Client's capabilities.sampling"],["Listing prompts","Server's capabilities.prompts"]]}

blocks.text: This check-before-use pattern means there is no single moment where negotiation 'concludes' with a computed intersection stored somewhere, instead, each side's declared capabilities are simply consulted every time a decision to use an optional feature comes up, for as long as the session lasts.

Some implementations do compute and cache an effective view once, right after initialization, purely as a convenience so the check-before-use logic scattered across the codebase has one obvious place to look, but this is an implementation detail layered on top of the architecture, not something the protocol itself defines or requires.

There is no automatic rejection just because two sides support different features, a mismatch simply means the unsupported feature is never used during that session, not that the session itself fails.
6. Capabilities Describe Support, Not Obligation

Declaring a capability means a side is able to handle that kind of message, it does not mean the other side is required to use it. A server declaring support for resource subscriptions does not force any client to actually subscribe to anything, the capability is an offer, not a mandate.

This distinction matters because a session can be perfectly healthy and useful even when very few optional capabilities are declared on either side, the baseline functionality, tools, resources, and prompts at their simplest, does not depend on any of the richer optional capabilities being present at all.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Declaration","What it means","What it does not mean"],"rows":[["Server declares resources.subscribe","Server can handle subscribe requests","Every client must subscribe to something"],["Client declares sampling","Client can handle sampling requests","The server must send sampling requests"]]}

blocks.text: Declaring a capability means readiness, not a promise it will be used every single time, a server offering resources still might handle a session where the client never actually reads one.
7. What Happens on a Capability Mismatch

blocks.alt: A capability mismatch leads to a graceful fallback

blocks.text: When one side lacks a capability the other would have liked to use, there is no error, no failed handshake, negotiation itself always succeeds. The side that wanted the missing feature simply avoids using it for the rest of the session, a client that wanted subscriptions but is talking to a server without that capability just falls back to plain, unsubscribed resource reads.

blocks.title: A mismatch is a graceful reduction, not a failure
blocks.content: The architecture is built so that a mismatch on an optional capability degrades functionality, not the session itself, initialization completing successfully never depends on both sides supporting the exact same optional features.

blocks.text: This graceful handling is what allows the MCP ecosystem to evolve over time, a server author can add a brand-new optional capability without breaking every existing client that has not been updated to use it yet, older clients simply never notice the new capability exists.

This is a meaningfully different design choice from systems where a version or feature mismatch aborts a connection outright, MCP treats an optional feature gap as something to route around gracefully rather than something worth failing an entire session over.

blocks.text: 8. Attempting to Use an Undeclared Capability

If, despite the negotiated capabilities, one side sends a request depending on something the other never declared, the receiving side responds with an error rather than silently ignoring or mishandling it. This is a defensive check on top of the negotiation itself, not a substitute for checking capabilities before sending a request in the first place.
9. Versioned Capability Sets

blocks.alt: Capability set v1 leads to capability set v2

blocks.text: Capabilities are declared alongside a protocolVersion string, and what a given capability field even means can, in principle, evolve between protocol versions. A client and server on different versions still negotiate successfully as long as they can agree on a mutually understood version, with capability meanings interpreted according to that agreed version.

This is precisely why the protocolVersion field is sent alongside capabilities rather than assumed, without it, a capability field could theoretically be interpreted two different ways by two implementations built against two different versions of the specification.

blocks.title: Version negotiation is a small negotiation of its own
blocks.content: Agreeing on a protocolVersion happens as part of the same initialize exchange, a client proposes a version it supports, and a server either accepts it or responds with a version it supports instead, before capabilities on that agreed version are even considered.

blocks.text: This versioning applies at the level of the whole protocol as well as individual capabilities, a server can support an older baseline while still adding a handful of newer, optional capabilities on top.
10. Sub-Capabilities Within a Category

Several capability categories break down further into specific sub-features, resources.subscribe and resources.listChanged are both part of the broader resources capability but can be declared independently, a server might support listing and reading resources without supporting live subscriptions to changes.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Capability","Sub-feature","Meaning"],"rows":[["resources","subscribe","Server supports resources/subscribe for change notifications"],["resources","listChanged","Server notifies when the overall resource list changes"],["prompts","listChanged","Server notifies when the overall prompt list changes"]]}

blocks.text: This finer granularity means a client cannot simply check whether a server supports resources broadly, it has to check the specific sub-feature it actually needs, checking only the top-level resources field would incorrectly assume subscription support that was never declared.
11. Capabilities Are Fixed for the Life of the Session

blocks.alt: A capability stays fixed for the session lifetime

blocks.text: Once initialization completes, neither side renegotiates capabilities mid-session, if a server's underlying functionality genuinely changes, adding subscription support it did not have before, that change only takes effect the next time a session is established, a fresh initialize handshake with updated declarations.

This fixed-for-the-session property is consistent with the same principle covered in Session Management, a reconnect always produces a brand new session with a brand new initialize handshake, capabilities are simply one more piece of state that gets re-established fresh rather than carried over.

blocks.title: A practical consequence
blocks.content: If a server gains a new feature while a client is still connected, that client will not see it until it reconnects and negotiates again.

blocks.text: 12. Negotiation Is Scoped Per Session

Just as covered in Session Management, capability negotiation happens independently for every session, a host connected to three servers, described in Multi-Server Architecture, negotiates three separate times, and one server declaring rich capabilities has no bearing whatsoever on what another server declares.

A host aggregating tools and resources from several servers, as described in Multi-Server Architecture, has to track each server's negotiated capabilities separately rather than assuming a single, shared capability set applies uniformly across every connection.
A host managing several independent server connections negotiates separately with each one, one server capability set never influences or leaks into another.
13. Forward Compatibility Through Optional Capabilities

blocks.alt: A required capability is compared against an optional capability

blocks.text: Treating every capability beyond a small required baseline as optional is what lets the protocol grow without breaking existing implementations. A brand new capability introduced in a future version of the specification is simply another field an older client or server never declares, and never checks for, everything continues working exactly as it did before that capability existed.

blocks.title: This is the same idea as feature detection on the web
blocks.content: A browser checking whether a JavaScript API exists before using it, rather than assuming every browser supports every feature, is the same defensive pattern capability negotiation applies to MCP sessions.

blocks.text: This is also why adding a genuinely new capability to the specification is a backward compatible change by design, existing servers and clients simply never declare it, and nothing about their behavior needs to change just because the option now exists somewhere in the ecosystem.
14. What Belongs in the Required Baseline Versus What Is Optional

A small set of behaviors, the initialize handshake itself, basic error responses, ping style liveness checks, are not gated behind capability declarations at all, every implementation is expected to support them unconditionally. Everything beyond that baseline, tools, resources, prompts, sampling, and their various sub-features, is explicitly optional and subject to negotiation.

blocks.text: 15. Worked Example: A Client Adapting to a Limited Server
Trace what happens when a client that supports resource subscriptions connects to a server that does not.

items: 1. Client sends initialize declaring sampling support, among other things.
2. Server responds declaring capabilities.resources with no subscribe field set.
3. Client checks the server's declared capabilities before offering a "watch this file" feature to the user.
4. Finding no subscribe support, the client disables that feature for this particular server.
5. The client still offers plain resource reads, since that baseline capability was declared.
6. The session proceeds normally for the rest of its life, with subscriptions simply never used against this server.

blocks.text: This adaptive behavior is exactly what lets the same client code work smoothly against both a rich, fully featured server and a minimal, simple one.
16. Common Mistakes in Capability Negotiation

items: Sending a request that depends on a capability without first checking whether the other side actually declared it.
Treating a missing optional capability as a fatal error instead of a normal, gracefully handled case.
Assuming capabilities negotiated with one server apply to a different server entirely.
Trying to renegotiate capabilities mid-session instead of establishing a fresh session when functionality changes.
Confusing a declared capability with a guarantee that the other side will actually use it.

blocks.text: A further common mistake is negotiating once and then never re-checking after a reconnect, a fresh session always deserves a fresh negotiation, even against the same server.
17. Practice: Write a Capability Check

Given a stored record of a server's negotiated capabilities from initialize, write the check a client should run before calling resources/subscribe, and decide what the client should do instead if that capability was never declared.
Key Takeaway

Capability negotiation happens once, during initialize, as each side declares what it supports, and every subsequent decision to use a feature is simply a check against those declarations, with a missing capability handled as a graceful fallback rather than a failure, for the entire fixed lifetime of that one session.

This closes out the MCP Architecture module, having covered how messages actually travel, how sessions and state are managed, the full request-response path, and how multiple servers and their capabilities fit together.
